article.title: LLVM 23 Cuts Compile Times 6.75% and Speeds Up Its Own Build by 45% With Precompiled Headers
article.summary: LLVM 23.1.0, released August 25, brings a 6.75% -O3 compile-time cut and precompiled headers that shrink LLVM/Clang build times by roughly 45%.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

LLVM 23.1.0 [was published](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/releases/tag/llvmorg-23.1.0) on August 25, with [official release notes](https://releases.llvm.org/23.1.0/docs/ReleaseNotes.html) documenting the changes across the compiler infrastructure project's IR, backends, tools, and bindings. Alongside the feature changes, LLVM contributor Alexis Engelke published a detailed technical account, ["Compile-Time Improvements in LLVM 23"](https://aengelke.net/llvm23-ct.html), describing how the new release achieves a compile-time reduction of 6.75% (10.53% for the sqlite3 benchmark) in -O3 builds, plus a roughly 45% cut to the time it takes to build LLVM and Clang themselves.

## What We Know

According to [Engelke's writeup](https://aengelke.net/llvm23-ct.html), the 6.75% overall compile-time improvement is not the product of one large change but the sum of dozens of small optimizations across LLVM's internals, measured using the stage2-O3 configuration on the LLVM compile-time-tracker.

Several of the largest individual gains came from LLVM's core data structures, [as detailed on the site](https://aengelke.net/llvm23-ct.html):

- LLVM's hash tables saw three changes: switching DenseMap from quadratic probing to linear probing with improved deletion (-1.27%), storing DenseMap occupancy in a compact bit array instead of reserved empty/tombstone keys, and moving the hash function from CityHash to xxh3 (-0.18%).
- SmallVector's `push_back` grow path was moved out-of-line to permit tail-call optimization, cutting instructions by 0.50%.
- The dominator tree's internal representation changed from a vector of children to a child-sibling layout (-0.13%) and adopted a bump allocator for its nodes (-0.50%), reducing calls to malloc and free.
- IR's `successors()` function was reimplemented as an iterator over a range of Uses (-0.21%), part of a larger effort that also split the `Br` opcode into separate unconditional and conditional branch opcodes.

On the backend side, GlobalISel — the instruction-selection framework intended to eventually replace FastISel — narrowed its performance gap on AArch64 at the -O0 optimization level, where GlobalISel is the default. Its end-to-end slowdown relative to FastISel fell from 12.71% to 9.39% overall, and from 31.81% to 26.13% on the sqlite3 benchmark, [per the article](https://aengelke.net/llvm23-ct.html).

Clang itself picked up targeted fixes, including lowering the density threshold at which SimplifyCFG generates static lookup tables from switch statements, from 40% down to 10%, which sped up compilation of C++ programs that hit that code path.

Separately from per-compile speed, LLVM 23 changes how the project itself is built. LLVM now [uses precompiled headers](https://aengelke.net/llvm23-ct.html) for nearly all of its compilation units, cutting LLVM and Clang's own build times by roughly 45%. Engelke's article states that compiling LLVM was previously very front-end intensive — parsing the C++ standard library and LLVM's Support headers repeatedly consumed more than 80% of build time even in release builds — and that precompiled headers bring front-end time down to about 55%. Five precompiled headers now cover LLVM Support (-14.73%), LLVM Core (-12.70%), LLVM CodeGen (-6.33%), clangAST (-13.85%), and clangCodeGen (-8.12%), individually measured on compile-time-tracker. The precompiled-header build is enabled by default when building with MSVC or Clang, but disabled for GCC, because GCC does not cache the additional template instantiations the approach requires and its precompiled-header files are comparatively large, according to the article.

The precompiled-header approach originated as [an RFC Engelke posted](https://discourse.llvm.org/t/rfc-use-pre-compiled-headers-to-speed-up-llvm-build-by-1-5-2x/89345) to the LLVM Discourse forum on December 31, 2025, which pitched the idea as capable of reducing LLVM build times by roughly 1.5 to 2x and improving stage2-clang build times by about 40% on compile-time-tracker — figures that describe the original proposal rather than the final numbers reported for the shipped LLVM 23 implementation.

According to [Engelke's acknowledgements](https://aengelke.net/llvm23-ct.html), most of the compile-time work in LLVM 23 was authored by Cullen Rhodes, Fangrui Song, and Engelke, with Nikita Popov — who hosts the compile-time-tracker service — reviewing most of the changes.

## What We Don't Know

Engelke's article notes that some further work is planned rather than finished: replacing LLVM's `llvm::cl` command-line option-parsing framework, which the article says is a major remaining source of shared-library startup overhead, is described as a bigger effort that will "hopefully happen for LLVM 24" rather than something completed in this release. The official LLVM 23.1.0 release notes catalog changes across the IR, backends, and tools but do not themselves quantify the compile-time or build-time improvements in the same benchmark detail as the technical writeup, so the specific percentages in this article are drawn from Engelke's account rather than the formal release documentation.

## Analysis

The LLVM 23 compile-time work illustrates a recurring theme in large compiler projects: rather than one headline optimization, meaningful speedups accumulate from many changes — hash-table internals, allocator behavior, iterator implementations, and build tooling — each contributing a fraction of a percent. The build-time change from precompiled headers is arguably the more consequential shift for day-to-day LLVM development, since it affects contributors compiling the compiler itself rather than end users compiling their own code with it.

LLVM 23 follows [LLVM 22](/article/2026-04/06-llvm-22-ships-distributed-thinlto-named-loops-for-c2y-and-webassembly-debugging-in-its-densest-release-yet), which shipped in February with production-ready Distributed ThinLTO and C2y named-loop support in Clang, continuing the project's roughly six-month major-release cadence.
